paragraphs: The paper studies how to identify the best option when each evaluation produces an uncertain but bounded reward. In the multi-armed bandit formulation, options are called arms, and repeated evaluations help estimate their average rewards. The goal here is best-arm identification: gathering evidence to determine which option has the highest mean.

The proposed algorithm combines lil-UCB and KL-LUCB, aiming to bring their favorable properties into one procedure. Its main theoretical ingredient is a new confidence bound for the mean of a bounded distribution. The bound is anytime, meaning it supports uncertainty assessment as observations accumulate, rather than being designed only for one predetermined sample count.

The authors relate this result to law-of-the-iterated-logarithm-style bounds previously developed for sub-Gaussian distributions. They also test the method numerically using the New Yorker Cartoon Caption Contest. This connects the statistical problem to crowdsourcing, where many candidate captions must be compared through noisy evaluations, and the experiments support the theoretical results.
neurips-2017-a-kl-lucb-algorithm-for-lar.tldr: A hybrid bandit algorithm uses a new anytime confidence bound to identify the best option from noisy, bounded evaluations.

paragraphs: This paper considers several related learning tasks that receive data over time. A learner can ask a human for a label, but doing so for every uncertain example ignores information already available from other tasks. The proposed approach treats those other learners as peers that may supply a sufficiently confident answer.

For each task, the algorithm first checks whether peer knowledge is adequate. It can combine peers using weights based on task similarity, or consult the single most similar task. When confidence is sufficient, it uses the peer-provided label. Otherwise, it asks the human oracle, reserving human input for cases that peers cannot resolve confidently.

The authors prove a mistake bound relative to the best linear predictor chosen in hindsight. Experiments on three multitask benchmark datasets also show better performance than the tested alternatives, including treating tasks independently and relying only on oracle labels. Together, these results support selectively sharing information across tasks as a way to make online learning and human querying work together.
neurips-2017-active-learning-from-peers-.tldr: An online multitask learner consults confident peers before asking a human for labels, with theoretical and experimental support.

paragraphs: RankGAN changes the feedback used to train an adversarial language generator. Conventional GAN discriminators classify individual samples as real or generated. The paper argues that this binary judgment limits the feedback available for richly structured outputs such as sentences, where quality can be assessed through comparisons among multiple examples.

The proposed discriminator evaluates a collection containing human-written and machine-written sentences, using a reference group to assign relative ranking scores. This makes its assessment comparative: a sentence receives feedback in relation to other sentences, rather than only an isolated real-or-fake decision. The intended benefit is a more informative assessment that helps the generator improve.

The authors train RankGAN with a policy gradient technique and evaluate it on multiple public datasets. The reported experiments support the effectiveness of the approach for language generation. The contribution is therefore both a change in the discriminator's task and a training method that uses those ranking judgments to guide generation; the evidence concerns the evaluated language-generation settings.
neurips-2017-adversarial-ranking-for-lan.tldr: RankGAN trains a language generator using relative rankings of human and generated sentences instead of binary real-or-fake judgments.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter tuning can require many expensive model fits, yet a selection procedure may ultimately retain only its best configuration. This paper asks whether the other fitted results can contribute to prediction. Its motivation is that uncertainty remains about which settings are best, and repeatedly optimizing against validation data also creates a risk of overfitting that data.

The proposed method, empirical Bayes for hyperparameter averaging, uses more samples from the hyperparameter selection process to average over uncertainty. Instead of committing all predictive weight to one selected setting, it incorporates information from multiple settings. This makes the results of the search useful beyond identifying a single winner.

In two experiments involving latent Dirichlet allocation and deep latent Gaussian models, the method predicts held-out data better than Bayesian optimization. The authors also suggest that this approach could simplify evaluation and deployment by removing the need for a separate validation dataset and hyperparameter selection procedure. That broader simplification is presented as a possibility motivated by the method and its experimental results.
neurips-2017-an-empirical-bayes-approach.tldr: Empirical Bayes hyperparameter averaging reuses multiple tuning results and improves held-out prediction in two reported experiments.

paragraphs: The paper studies optimization problems in which a learner competes with an adversary. These naturally lead to saddle-point formulations, where the two sides optimize in opposing directions. For adversarial prediction with multivariate losses, the resulting problem can be extremely large, making both its representation and its optimization expensive.

The authors first use suitable sufficient statistics to reduce the problem size exponentially. They then adapt an existing stochastic variance-reduced algorithm so that it can use any Bregman divergence. This broadens the geometry available to the optimizer: progress need not be measured using only the usual Euclidean notion of distance.

The analysis retains the algorithm's linear convergence rate. For adversarial prediction, choosing KL divergence can additionally provide a speedup by a factor equal to the number of examples compared with the Euclidean alternative. Experiments on adversarial prediction and LPboosting support the theoretical findings. The two contributions address complementary bottlenecks: sufficient statistics shrink the problem, while the choice of divergence can make solving the reduced problem faster.
neurips-2017-bregman-divergence-for-stoc.tldr: Sufficient statistics and Bregman-based variance reduction accelerate adversarial prediction while preserving a linear convergence guarantee.

paragraphs: A learning system that explores new decisions may temporarily perform worse than an established strategy. This paper studies that deployment concern in contextual linear bandits, where decisions use contextual information and learning must balance exploration with performance. It defines safety through comparison with a baseline strategy.

The proposed conservative linear UCB algorithm, CLUCB, minimizes regret while maintaining performance above a fixed percentage of the baseline's performance throughout time. The percentage-based constraint is the precise safety requirement. It gives the learner a specified performance floor while still allowing it to seek better decisions.

The authors prove a regret bound with two components. One grows with the time horizon like a bound for standard linear UCB; the other is a constant term representing the cost of satisfying the conservative constraint. This decomposition identifies an additional cost of caution that does not itself keep growing with the horizon in the bound. Experiments demonstrate the stated safety behavior and support the theoretical analysis.
neurips-2017-conservative-contextual-lin.tldr: CLUCB learns contextual decisions while maintaining a fixed fraction of baseline performance, with a constant additional conservatism term in its regret bound.

paragraphs: This paper investigates why kernel methods can struggle on large datasets even when their underlying function spaces are expressive. It separates the capabilities of a shallow model from the behavior of the optimization algorithm used to train it. The central finding concerns gradient descent with smooth kernels.

The analysis shows that after a polynomial number of gradient descent iterations, only a vanishingly small part of the function space is reachable. This restricts what training can approximate and creates excessive regularization. The obstacle is algorithmic and persists even with infinite data, so collecting more examples alone does not remove the identified problem.

The authors propose EigenPro, a preconditioning method based on a small number of approximately computed eigenvectors. It adds inexpensive approximate second-order information and is compatible with stochastic gradient descent. The method can also be interpreted as learning a kernel suited to gradient descent. Reported large-data results show major convergence improvements and match or improve published kernel-method results using a small fraction of their computational budget.
neurips-2017-diving-into-the-shallows-a-.tldr: EigenPro addresses an optimization bottleneck in smooth kernel learning through inexpensive spectral preconditioning.

paragraphs: A network's links can reflect different kinds of hidden organization. The paper focuses on two widely used explanations: stochastic block models, which describe block structure, and small-world or latent-space models, which describe nodes through latent positions. Selecting an inappropriate model can lead an analysis to report patterns created by its own assumptions.

The authors develop a unified algorithm using techniques from kernel learning, spectral graph theory, and nonlinear dimensionality reduction. It is designed to discover latent structure in sparse graphs under either of the two model families. The abstract identifies it as the first statistically sound polynomial-time algorithm covering both settings.

The output depends on the network's generating model. For a stochastic block model, the algorithm returns blocks; for a small-world model, it estimates each node's latent position. This matters because the method can recover two different forms of organization within one framework. Its stated coverage is specifically these two model families, so the result does not establish correctness for every possible network-generating process.
neurips-2017-from-which-world-is-your-gr.tldr: A unified polynomial-time algorithm recovers blocks or latent positions in sparse graphs generated by two major network models.

paragraphs: Activity recorded from many neurons can look high-dimensional even when a small number of hidden variables organizes it. This paper addresses cases where linear descriptions obscure that simpler structure. Its key idea is to allow nonlinear tuning curves, so neurons can respond nonlinearly to a shared low-dimensional latent state.

The Poisson Gaussian-Process Latent Variable Model combines Poisson observations of spikes with two Gaussian processes. One governs the latent variable over time, and the other governs the nonlinear tuning curves connecting latent states to neural responses. To fit the model, the authors introduce a decoupled Laplace approximation that optimizes the latent trajectory while marginalizing over the tuning curves.

The proposed inference method improves convergence speed and accuracy over previous Laplace-based methods in the reported comparisons. Applied to hippocampal place-cell recordings, the model also compares favorably with several earlier structure-discovery methods, including approaches using variational autoencoders. The findings support nonlinear mappings as a way to reveal compact structure that may be difficult to recognize through linear dimensionality.
neurips-2017-gaussian-process-based-nonl.tldr: A nonlinear Gaussian-process model reveals low-dimensional structure in neural spike trains and introduces faster, more accurate approximate inference.

paragraphs: The paper connects accelerated optimization with numerical methods for solving differential equations. Its starting point is gradient flow, the continuous-time equation describing motion along the negative gradient of an objective. An optimization algorithm can be understood as a sequence of discrete updates that approximates such continuous motion.

The authors show that accelerated methods arise as particular multistep integration schemes applied to this basic gradient-flow equation. Multistep schemes use information from multiple steps when constructing an update. Using classical conditions from numerical analysis, the paper derives a class of such schemes that includes accelerated optimization algorithms.

This viewpoint places the explanation for acceleration in the integration method. The schemes can advance the differential equation with larger step sizes, which the authors offer as an intuitive explanation of faster optimization. The contribution is a mathematical connection and a derivation of a family of methods. It also provides a way to study acceleration using established numerical-analysis ideas while keeping the underlying differential equation as ordinary gradient flow.
neurips-2017-integration-methods-and-opt.tldr: Accelerated optimization can be derived as multistep numerical integration of basic gradient flow, with larger integration steps offering intuition for acceleration.

paragraphs: The paper studies feature selection: choosing a subset of input variables that carries as much predictive information about an outcome as possible. Its approach uses kernel-based measures of independence to assess that information. This connects the selection problem to statistical relationships between the response and the candidate covariates.

Building on kernel dimension reduction, the authors formulate selection as a constrained optimization problem involving the trace of a conditional covariance operator. The conditional aspect makes the criterion concern what remains uncertain about the response after accounting for selected inputs. Minimizing this quantity provides a mathematical target for finding a predictive subset of variables.

The authors prove several consistency results and compare the procedure with other leading feature-selection algorithms on synthetic and real datasets. The reported comparisons are favorable. These contributions address both the statistical justification of the selection criterion and its practical behavior: the theory supports the procedure through consistency results, while the experiments show how it performs on the datasets examined.
neurips-2017-kernel-feature-selection-vi.tldr: A kernel-based feature-selection method minimizes conditional covariance to identify predictive subsets, with consistency results and favorable empirical comparisons.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to recover the distribution of hidden probabilities across a population. Each entity has an unknown probability between zero and one, and the observation for that entity is a binomial count from t trials. The target is the population's distribution of probabilities, rather than an accurate estimate of every individual probability.

Simply forming the distribution of the observed success proportions produces error of order 1 divided by the square root of t in earth mover distance. The authors show that, when the population size n is sufficiently large, their approach achieves error of order 1 divided by t. They also establish that this improved rate is information-theoretically optimal.

The results extend to multidimensional parameters, allowing each population member to have several associated quantities. Experiments across several datasets demonstrate useful recovery in practice, with applications involving politics, sports analytics, and offspring gender ratios. The central implication is that learning the population distribution can be substantially more accurate than directly collecting noisy individual estimates into a histogram.
neurips-2017-learning-populations-of-par.tldr: With sufficiently many entities, a population's hidden probability distribution can be recovered at an optimal error rate of order 1/t.

paragraphs: This paper studies bandit learning when changing actions carries a cost. A fixed, known metric specifies the cost of moving between each pair of actions. The learner therefore pays both the loss of its chosen actions and the expense of switching, making the geometry of the action space part of the learning problem.

For k actions over T rounds, the authors give an efficient algorithm and a matching characterization of expected minimax regret, up to logarithmic factors. The rate is the larger of C^(1/3)T^(2/3) and sqrt(kT), where C depends on the metric's covering numbers. This connects learning difficulty to how the action space can be covered at different distance scales.

The result includes uniform switching costs and interval metrics as special cases. For infinite metric spaces with Lipschitz losses and Minkowski dimension d at least one, the tight rate is T^((d+1)/(d+2)), again up to logarithmic factors. That rate is already necessary without switching costs, showing that movement costs do not worsen its order in this stated setting.
neurips-2017-multi-armed-bandits-with-me.tldr: The paper characterizes optimal bandit regret when switching costs follow a known metric, linking difficulty to the action space's geometry.

paragraphs: Sequential prediction often involves more than one criterion: a predictor may need to improve an objective while keeping another measure within a constraint. This paper extends a multi-objective learning framework beyond independent, identically distributed observations. Its setting allows observations to depend on earlier observations.

The extension assumes a stationary and ergodic process. These assumptions permit dependence while retaining stable statistical structure and meaningful long-run behavior. They are central to the result: the paper addresses dependent data within this process class, rather than arbitrary changes in the sequence's statistical behavior.

The authors establish a long-run lower bound for any prediction strategy and construct an algorithm whose predictions achieve the optimal solution while satisfying a continuous, convex constraining criterion. The lower bound identifies the performance benchmark, and the algorithm shows that it is attainable in the stated framework. This brings multi-objective sequential prediction into a setting where observations can be connected over time while preserving a theoretical account of both optimality and constraint satisfaction.
neurips-2017-multi-objective-non-paramet.tldr: A multi-objective sequential predictor achieves the stated optimum under continuous convex constraints for stationary, ergodic data.

paragraphs: Fast similarity search often uses quantization to represent high-dimensional vectors compactly. This paper identifies a difficulty for product quantization when vector norms, or lengths, vary greatly. The issue is especially relevant to residual vectors, which represent what remains after a coarse vector quantizer has approximated the original data.

The proposed multiscale method learns a separate scalar quantizer for the scales of residual norms. This gives differences in magnitude an explicit role in the representation. All parameters are learned together with stochastic gradient descent to minimize overall quantization error, so the scale representation and the other quantization components are optimized toward the same objective.

The authors provide theoretical motivation and evaluate the method on two large public datasets. They report substantial recall improvements over existing leading methods, meaning the search retrieves more of the relevant neighbors in those comparisons. The findings support treating variation in vector magnitude as an important source of quantization error when designing compact representations for large-scale similarity search.
neurips-2017-multiscale-quantization-for.tldr: Learning residual-vector scales jointly with quantization improves similarity-search recall on two large datasets.

paragraphs: The paper examines a tension between two desirable properties of predictive models: calibrated probability estimates and reduced differences in error across population groups. Calibration concerns whether predicted probabilities correspond to observed outcomes. Error parity concerns whether groups experience comparable mistakes. These requirements place different demands on the same predictions.

The authors show that, in the framework they study, calibration is compatible only with a single error constraint, such as equal false-negative rates across groups. This restricts how far error equalization can go while preserving calibrated probabilities. The result makes the choice of which error requirement to impose mathematically consequential.

Even under that relaxation, the authors show that a satisfying algorithm is no better than randomizing a percentage of an existing classifier's predictions. Experiments on several datasets confirm the reported theoretical findings. The contribution identifies limits on simultaneously pursuing these particular statistical requirements, including the limited benefit available under the relaxation; it does not equate these requirements with every possible meaning of fairness.
neurips-2017-on-fairness-and-calibration.tldr: The paper establishes tensions between calibration and group error parity, including limits on the benefit of satisfying a single relaxed error constraint.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning a new task from one demonstration after training across many other tasks. It distinguishes a task from its individual instances: stacking blocks into one tower is a task, while different blocks and starting arrangements produce different instances. The goal is to transfer the demonstrated task to a new situation.

During training, the method receives pairs of demonstrations belonging to the same task. A neural network takes one demonstration and the current state as inputs, then predicts an action intended to reproduce the behavior of the second demonstration. This trains the network to use a demonstration as guidance across differing initial conditions.

At test time, the network receives one demonstration of a previously unseen task and is evaluated on new instances of that task. Experiments show that soft attention enables generalization to conditions and tasks absent from training. The authors anticipate broader capabilities with much more varied training, but a general system handling an overwhelming variety of tasks remains an aspiration beyond the reported result.
neurips-2017-one-shot-imitation-learning.tldr: Training across paired demonstrations enables a neural policy to use one demonstration of a new task and generalize to new instances.

paragraphs: The paper studies how many partial rankings are needed to recover an ordering focused on the best K items. Each observation ranks M items under a model based on Plackett-Luce preferences, with noisy perceived utilities reflecting underlying true utilities. The analysis characterizes the minimax-optimal sample requirement, which decreases in proportion to 1/M.

The proposed algorithm converts rankings of M items into pairwise information and applies a spectral method to the resulting data. Its analysis develops tight bounds on the largest individual estimation error. Such control matters because accurate overall estimates can still conceal an error large enough to disrupt the ordering near the top-K boundary.

Within slightly restricted regimes, the results show that the spectral method alone suffices, without an additional maximum-likelihood stage used in earlier pairwise work. Synthetic experiments confirm the 1/M sample-size scaling. Experiments on real data also suggest applicability beyond settings that fit the Plackett-Luce model, although that empirical observation does not extend the model-based optimality guarantee to all preference data.
neurips-2017-optimal-sample-complexity-o.tldr: A spectral ranking method achieves optimal sample scaling proportional to 1/M for M-item comparisons within the stated regimes.

paragraphs: Variational inference approximates a difficult posterior by optimizing a more manageable distribution. This paper interprets generalized-divergence versions of black-box variational inference as biased importance-sampling estimates of marginal likelihood. That interpretation exposes a trade-off between obtaining a tighter bound and keeping the gradient estimates used for optimization sufficiently stable.

Drawing on perturbation theory from statistical physics, the authors construct a family of variational bounds indexed by an odd integer K. At K equal to one, the family recovers the standard KL bound. As K tends to infinity, it converges to the exact marginal likelihood. The proposed reparameterization gradients also have lower variance than those associated with alpha divergences.

Experiments on Gaussian processes and variational autoencoders show more mass-covering approximations, meaning the fitted distributions represent posterior probability more broadly. The resulting posterior covariances are closer to the true posterior, and held-out likelihoods improve. These findings connect the new objectives to both uncertainty estimation and predictive performance, while exact marginal-likelihood recovery is specifically a limiting statement.
neurips-2017-perturbative-black-box-vari.tldr: Perturbation-based variational bounds balance approximation and gradient noise, improving posterior coverage and held-out likelihood in reported experiments.

paragraphs: The paper addresses interpretability in sequential decision making with text. A system may choose effective actions while leaving users unable to see the patterns behind those choices. Q-LDA is a probabilistic model intended to expose latent structure in these decision processes while also pursuing strong reward performance.

The model adapts latent topic modeling to the goal of maximizing total reward. This connects hidden patterns in text to the sequential decision objective, rather than treating text structure as a separate descriptive task. The authors also establish a connection between approximate maximum-likelihood estimation for Q-LDA and Q-learning, linking probabilistic model fitting with a familiar reinforcement-learning algorithm.

Experiments in text games show that the method can uncover latent patterns and achieve rewards described as state of the art. These are complementary findings: the model provides a mechanism for examining decision-related structure while remaining competitive at the task itself. The stated interpretability result concerns discovering latent patterns; it does not establish that those patterns are proven causal explanations of decisions.
neurips-2017-q-lda-uncovering-latent-pat.tldr: Q-LDA connects reward-oriented topic modeling with Q-learning to reveal latent decision patterns and achieve strong text-game rewards.

paragraphs: Many regression methods optimize squared error, which can make them sensitive to outliers and heavy-tailed noise. This paper instead studies regularized modal regression. Its target is the conditional mode: the most likely response value for given inputs. Changing that target provides an alternative basis for estimation in difficult noise conditions.

The proposed model performs both function estimation and variable selection. The authors characterize its robustness to outliers, heavy-tailed noise, and skewed noise. Their theoretical analysis covers approximation of the conditional mode function, sparsity in the selected variables, and robustness, linking the predictive target with the ability to identify a smaller set of relevant inputs.

The method is also applied to cognitive impairment prediction using data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative cohort, where the authors report an improvement. This application demonstrates the approach in the studied prediction setting. The broader methodological contribution is a statistically analyzed alternative to squared-error regression that combines a modal prediction target with regularization and variable selection.
neurips-2017-regularized-modal-regressio.tldr: Regularized modal regression combines robust estimation and variable selection, with a reported improvement in cognitive impairment prediction.

paragraphs: The paper formulates explanation of a black-box classifier as selecting a limited set of elements to maximize an explanation objective. The limit on the number selected is a cardinality constraint. To make this selection efficient as candidates arrive, the authors develop a streaming algorithm.

Its theoretical guarantee applies when the objective is weakly submodular and the stream arrives in random order. Under those conditions, the algorithm achieves a constant-factor approximation to the best objective value. The authors identify this as the first such guarantee for the function class and also show that a corresponding guarantee is impossible for worst-case stream ordering.

In an application to Inception V3 predictions, the algorithm produces explanations similar to those from LIME while running ten times faster. The result connects streaming optimization to practical explanation speed. The ordering distinction is essential to interpreting the theory: the positive guarantee relies on random order, while the negative result shows why that condition cannot simply be discarded.
neurips-2017-streaming-weak-submodularit.tldr: A streaming explanation algorithm has a random-order approximation guarantee and produces similar Inception V3 explanations ten times faster than LIME.

paragraphs: Embeddings describe relationships among items, but those relationships may vary across groups. A word can be used differently across political affiliations or research areas, and grocery co-purchases can change with the season. This paper develops structured exponential family embeddings to capture such group-dependent patterns.

The method allows embeddings to vary across related groups while sharing statistical information between them. The authors develop two sharing strategies, hierarchical modeling and amortization. This sharing is central to the approach: each group's representation can reflect its own patterns while drawing on information available across the collection of groups.

The empirical studies examine Congressional speeches by state and party, abstracts from different ArXiv sections, and seasonal shopping baskets. The resulting embeddings support group-specific interpretations of word usage and predict held-out data better than the unstructured exponential family embedding model in the reported evaluations. The findings show how modeling group variation and sharing information can jointly improve both the interpretation of relationships and predictive performance.
neurips-2017-structured-embedding-models.tldr: Structured embeddings share information across related groups while capturing group-specific patterns in language and shopping data.

paragraphs: The paper investigates embeddings built from structured random matrices whose rows are orthogonal. These transformations can serve applications such as dimensionality reduction and kernel approximation. The main question is how the combination of matrix structure and orthogonality affects the accuracy and computational speed of those representations.

For the Johnson-Lindenstrauss transform and the angular kernel, the authors show that suitable matrix choices provide guaranteed improvements in accuracy, speed, or both compared with earlier methods. They also introduce matrices with complex-valued entries and report significant additional accuracy improvements. The guarantee therefore concerns selected constructions and the stated applications, rather than every structured random matrix.

The authors develop geometric and Markov-chain-based perspectives to explain the benefits. Empirical results further suggest that the approach may be helpful across a wider range of applications. The paper thus combines targeted guarantees, new matrix constructions, and explanatory viewpoints, while distinguishing the proven improvements in specific settings from the broader usefulness suggested by experiments.
neurips-2017-the-unreasonable-effectiven.tldr: Selected structured random orthogonal embeddings improve accuracy or speed in dimensionality reduction and kernel approximation.

paragraphs: Triangle GAN addresses learning relationships between two domains when examples from each domain are available but only a few are paired. The task is to learn their joint distribution, including which examples correspond across domains. This setting supports using limited correspondence supervision alongside the separate collections of samples.

The architecture has two generators and two discriminators. Each generator learns a conditional distribution in one direction between the domains. Together, the discriminators distinguish three kinds of pairs: real pairs and the two types of generated pairs. Adversarial training therefore evaluates the correspondence produced by both directions within a shared learning setup.

Under mild assumptions, the authors prove that the joint distributions represented by the generators concentrate toward the data distribution. Experiments cover image-label, image-image, and image-attribute relationships, with favorable results on semi-supervised classification, image translation, and attribute-based generation. The findings support the framework across these tested tasks, while the theoretical distribution-matching conclusion retains its stated assumptions.
neurips-2017-triangle-generative-adversa.tldr: Triangle GAN learns bidirectional relationships between domains using few paired examples and a three-way adversarial comparison.
